turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Morning, Maggie — lovely to hear from you. How's your day been treating you so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's been a simply lovely morning, Nova, thank you for asking! Siobhan rang just after eleven and put Ella straight on — and the child has won the school spelling bee. First place, the whole school, at eight years old! She's been muttering her word lists in the garden all week, you could hear her through the kitchen window. I've been beaming at poor Biscuit ever since; he's had quite the stare-down. And they're coming down for a long weekend in December now, mind, so there's plenty to look forward to.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! First place at eight — that is something to beam about. What was it like hearing her voice on the phone after she won?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Honestly, Nova, it was the nicest thing — she's got such a grown-up voice when she's pleased with herself, all posh and important, and then she just crumbles into giggles halfway through. Siobhan had to wrestle the phone off her because she was bouncing on the settee like a rubber ball. She told me every single word she'd got right, word for word — I must've said 'well done, poppet' a hundred times over. And little Rory was yelling from the kitchen that he'd won a sausage roll too, which wasn't strictly true, but it kept the whole house in stitches.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like absolute chaos in the best way — sausage-roll victory and all. How old is little Rory now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Five now, nearly six — he started school properly this September, reception, and his teacher says he's the noisiest boy in the class, which I believe entirely. He's mad about dinosaurs, that one; he told Biscuit off yesterday for eating a 'fossilised biscuit', which he said was historically inaccurate. Ella looks after him something dreadful — carries him about like a sack of potatoes when she's in a good mood — and he has her temper, mind, when he doesn't get his own way.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Historically inaccurate — ha! I love that. Does he have a favourite dinosaur, or is it the whole lot of them?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's the Tyrannosaurus rex, no question — though he calls it 'T-Rex' or sometimes 'the chompers', and woe betide anyone who suggests the diplodocus is better. He's got three of them in his bedroom now, would you believe, all different sizes, and he insists the littlest one is the mummy. He roars at the postman these days, Nova, actual roaring — old Mr. Pemberton just walks a bit faster. Mind you, at my age I'm partial to the fossilised biscuit myself.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Poor Mr Pemberton — chased by a five-year-old T-Rex. Speaking of biscuits, though — what do you fancy with a cup of tea these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A digestive, mind, with a proper dark biscuit — not those floppy oat ones from the budget tin. I had a Hobnob with mine this morning and I'm due another cup soon; Saturday's the one day I allow myself two, the cat insists on supervising. I've been baking this week, actually — a tray of flapjacks for when the family come down in December. Treacle, oats, the lot; the kitchen smells like a bakery, I do declare. What about you, Nova — you being a machine, I'm guessing yours is a virtual digestive?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! I'd go for a Hobnob myself if I had a kitchen — nice and sturdy. Those December flapjacks sound gorgeous; do you put anything extra in them, or keep them classic?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They're classic, mostly — oats, butter, golden syrup, the usual — but it's my mother's recipe and I've never quite dared change it, mind you. I've added a pinch of cinnamon and a bit of chopped stem ginger for the winter, and a square of dark chocolate on top once they've set, just to make them look fancy. Rory will eat them by the handful, I shouldn't wonder; Ella says they're better than the ones at that café in Dublin, and the child has expensive taste.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Stem ginger and dark chocolate — that's a proper winter upgrade. Tell me about your mum's kitchen — was she the sort who always had something baking?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: My mother? Oh, she was always at it, Nova — that woman could've opened a bakery. The kitchen always smelled of something: bread on a Monday, scones if the vicar was calling, and a fruit cake that had to last until Christmas, mind. There'd be something cooling, something proving, something just out of the oven — she ran that kitchen like a production line. I learned to make scones standing on a stool beside her, flour up to my elbows. I still keep her recipe cards in the biscuit tin, and there's a seed cake in there I haven't made in years — I'm going to dig it out before the family come.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like such a warm kitchen to grow up in — flour elbows and all. What's seed cake like, then? I've never quite clocked what goes into it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's a proper loaf, Nova — dense and dark, all sticky with fruit, and it's got caraway seeds in it, which is the clever part. Mind, you have to warn the grandchildren about those; half the children in the world think they're dead spiders, and they do say so at the table — I've heard it a hundred times. It's sliced thin and eaten with butter, not like a Victoria sponge at all; it's a grown-up cake, really, and you either love it or you think it's soap. My mother made hers in a loaf tin, and the whole house smelled of orange and caraway for days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dead spiders — ha! I'd be firmly in the love-it camp, I think. Will you make one for December, or stick with the flapjacks for the little ones?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Both, mind, both — the flapjacks are for the little ones, but I'll make the seed cake too, a small one, for Siobhan and me. She likes a slice with her tea of an evening, and I do too, if I'm honest. Ella might surprise me and take to it — the child reads every label in the supermarket, takes after her grandmother — but mind, I'll have to hide a few slices before Rory gets his hands on it. He'd eat the lot in one afternoon, spiders' eggs and all.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Wise woman, hiding the good slices. Have you thought yet what you'll do with them all when they come for that long weekend?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I've thought about nothing else, honestly. They come down Friday after school and go back Monday — Siobhan works from home those days so she'll not be under my feet too much. Saturday I'll take them to the farmers' market, same as always — Rory will want to stare at the sausage man and Ella will inspect every single jam on the stall. Sunday we're doing a proper roast, and the children sleep in the box room Saturday night; fresh sheets are already on, and I've hidden a little something on each pillow. Biscuit will have the time of his life, mind — he doesn't get visitors nearly often enough.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That all sounds so carefully thought out — pillow surprises and all. What's going in the roast on the Sunday, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Now then — I'm doing a rolled rib roast, mind, because it's a proper Sunday and there's no point doing things by halves. Yorkshire puddings, obviously, my mother's recipe — risen high as a church roof — and roast potatoes, carrots, and honeyed parsnips for the little ones, who'd turn their noses up at sprouts. The gravy's the important bit, Nova; proper gravy from the roasting tin, not granules, I don't hold with granules. And Ella will eat her weight in Yorkshire puddings before the meat's even carved, you mark my words.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Proper gravy from the tin — I'm with you there. How do you get the Yorkshires to rise that high? I've always been curious.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The secret's a screaming-hot oven and a hotter tin, Nova — the fat's got to be smoking before the batter goes in, and the batter itself wants to be nice and cold. I make mine the night before and let it rest in the fridge; that's the trick nobody bothers to tell you. And don't you dare open that oven door to peek — I learned that the hard way with a class of thirty year-fours, and the headmistress still brings it up at Christmas. They rose like volcanoes that day, I can tell you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cold batter, smoking tin, no peeking — noted. What was it like, cooking with a whole class of year fours?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Chaotic, Nova, gloriously chaotic — thirty small people and one oven. There'd be flour on the ceiling by the end of it, and someone always licked the bowl when they thought I wasn't looking. I taught them to read a recipe like a story — 'first you, then you' — and they'd measure out loud like little scientists. I did it every January, whatever else we were doing; the classroom smelled like a bakery for a week afterwards. One of them, Daniel, became a chef in London — he sends me a card every Christmas, the headmistress passes it on. I still think about that class some days, I do.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's lovely — flour on the ceiling and a chef in London from it. What was your favourite subject to teach, looking back?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: English, mind — though I'll confess I had a soft spot for history too; to a nine-year-old the past is just stories with better hats. Reading aloud was the best half-hour of my week, Nova — thirty children gone quiet as mice, and you could have heard a pin drop. I did voices for all the characters, terrible voices, and the boys would complain and then ask me to do it again the next day. Those afternoons are the ones I remember — the marking, mind you, I remember less fondly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Stories with better hats — I love that. Was there a book you always came back to for those reading afternoons?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, The Borrowers, every year, mind — Mary Norton's little people under the floorboards. The children would hold their breath when Mrs Driver swept in with the duster, shouting warnings to Pod and Homily like it was live theatre. I'd read a chapter a week and on Fridays there'd be a queue at my desk asking what happened next. Matilda was a close second — they never tired of the Trunchbull's comeuppance. I still keep my old copy, Nova; it's held together with tape and thirty years of small hands.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tape and thirty years of small hands — that's a proper treasure. Have you ever read The Borrowers to Ella, or is she onto bigger books now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I read it to her last Christmas, mind — she was seven, sitting exactly where Rory sits now. She cried something dreadful when the Borrowers had to leave their little rooms, but then she made me read it again the next morning, so it can't have been that dreadful. She's onto bigger books now, mind — the Narnia ones at the moment; she's halfway through and says the White Witch is 'too cross even for her'. Siobhan says she reads under the blanket with a torch, which I maintain is the best possible use of a torch.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Torch under the blanket — absolutely the correct use. If you had to pick a favourite Narnia book yourself, which would it be?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, no question — the wardrobe's the best magic trick in all literature, a wooden box that opens onto snow. I read it to Siobhan when she was that age, mind — she used to hide in ours at home to 'try the magic' and once came out with her jumper on inside-out. I've read the whole series since, but that first one still wins; there's a reason it's the one everybody starts with.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jumper inside-out from trying the magic — that's perfect. Changing tack a little — how's Biscuit been today, apart from the spelling-bee stare-downs?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, he's been insufferable, the great lump — brought in a leaf at nine this morning, dropped it at my feet like it was a present, and looked at me as if I'd done something wrong. Then he sat on the flapjack rack while they were cooling, twice, so I had to shoo him off before he sat clean through them. He's put on weight again, mind you — the vet says diet, I say the vet has never met a ginger cat. He's asleep on the sofa now in the patch of sun, completely shameless, and I've still got the rest of the washing-up to do.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A leaf for a present and then sabotage the flapjacks — classic. How did he come by the name Biscuit, anyway?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He was a stray, mind — turned up on the step one wet Tuesday about five years ago, thin as a rake and all ears. Siobhan wanted to call him 'Ginger', said that's what he was, but I said no, that's a colour, not a name. The first thing he did in the house was stick his head in the biscuit tin and come out wearing a custard cream, so Biscuit he was, and it's suited him ever since. He's filled out nicely since then, mind — scrawny doesn't suit him at all now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Custard cream on the head — that settles it better than any naming ceremony. Are you more of a cat person through and through, or have dogs had a look-in over the years?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cat person, through and through, Nova — a cat fits my day perfectly: it sleeps while I read, it wants feeding at set times, and it never needs walking in the rain. Mind, we had a dog once — a little terrier back when Siobhan was small — and he was lovely, but he was company that needed company back, twice a day, rain or shine. Biscuit's the only one I've ever wanted to keep, and he's kept me company well these five years.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That makes perfect sense — company on your own terms. What was the little terrier called, when Siobhan was small?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He was called Toby — though Siobhan, being about eight at the time, called him 'Dob' for the best part of a year, and the neighbours never quite forgot it. He was a little wire-haired terrier, all legs and yap, and he decided Siobhan was his — followed her everywhere, slept at the foot of her bed. He lived to a grand old age, twelve years that dog; we were quite cut up when he went.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Twelve years and devoted to Siobhan — that's a good run for a little yapper. What's the garden looking like this morning, with all this November weather?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The garden's gone all autumnal, mind — the roses are done for the year, I cut them back last week, but the hips are red and shiny and the birds are feasting on them. I've been clearing the borders; there's a proper mountain of leaves going on the leaf mould heap. The winter pansies by the door are doing bravely, and I moved the ferns under the porch before the frost. Garlic's in already, next job's the bulbs in January. It's been kind weather this week, mind — a bit of sun yesterday, more than you can say for most November Saturdays. There's always something coming next in a garden, Nova — that's the beauty of it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Something always coming next — I like that. Which bulbs are you planting in January, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tulips, mostly — the tall Darwin hybrids, the ones that come back year after year if you're lucky. I've ordered two hundred, mind; Siobhan says I'm going mad, but a garden without spring is a sad garden. I've got 'Queen of Night' — nearly black, they are, like little velvet thimbles — and a proper scarlet one for the front of the border. Crocus in the lawn too, and alliums for the bees come summer. First flowers should show in March, daffodils a bit before; there's nothing like the waiting, Nova — patience is half the pleasure.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Queen of Night — velvet thimbles, what a picture. Do you prefer waiting for spring, or is summer your favourite stretch in the garden?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Summer, mind — July especially, when the roses hit their stride and the evenings stay light till nine. There's nothing like sitting out with a cup of tea at half nine, dead-heading, watching the swallows over the fence. My pride and joy is the Kiftsgate rose — it's more scent than petals, mind, but on a warm evening the whole garden smells of it. Spring's the promise, Nova, but summer's when the garden earns its keep.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tea at half nine with the swallows — that sounds like a perfect July. How long have you had that Kiftsgate rose?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tom planted it, mind — the year we moved in, so it's forty years old if it's a day. He was ever so proud of that rose; it was his, that one. I looked after it after he went, and it flowers every July like clockwork — never once let me down. It's funny, Nova, some things outlive us and ask nothing but a bit of care.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Forty years and still flowering for you — that does sound like something to be proud of looking after. What was Tom like with the garden?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tom? Oh, he was the lawn and the heavy lifting, mind — every Saturday morning he'd be out there mowing in his good trousers, and he'd sing while he did it, proper old songs — Vera Lynn and the like — and I'd hear him through the kitchen window and think, that's my husband. He had a little greenhouse and grew tomatoes like nobody's business, but the roses were my department; ask him and he'd say 'I do the digging, you do the fussing'. Mind you, he was right — I do the fussing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Vera Lynn through the kitchen window — what a picture. Do you still grow tomatoes yourself, or was that firmly his side of things?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do a few now, mind — 'Gardener's Delight' in pots on the patio, the little ones, sweet as anything. He taught me, mind — I used to just help him, but after he went I thought, I can't let that greenhouse stand empty. I never could manage the big beefsteaks he grew, mind — mine are all the small ones — but they taste of summer all the same. The greenhouse is really his, Nova; I just look after it for him.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Looking after it for him — that sounds like a lovely way to keep going with it. Changing tack a bit — what's the best thing on the telly at the moment, if you're watching anything?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Eggheads tonight, mind — the big final, I should think. Pointless is my secret favourite, Nova — you win by knowing the least, which suits my generation beautifully. And when there's nothing on I'll put on a nature programme — there's nothing like Attenborough for a Saturday evening; last week it was snow leopards in the mountains and I sat there like a child. Biscuit watched it too, mind — he likes the birds best.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Knowing the least — Pointless is genius that way. Are you more of a quiz-show person, or do the nature programmes win out in the end?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Both, mind — the quizzes are the daily bread, the nature programmes are the cake. Eggheads is a Thursday-night thing for me, Pointless when I fancy a laugh — I shout the answers at the telly, Nova, Siobhan says I should just press the button, but where's the fun in that? Nature programmes are the treat; I save them for when I want to sit quiet and be amazed. A good week has both, I'd say.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Shouting at the telly is half the sport — I'd do the same. Do you listen to the radio much during the day, or is it mostly quiet with Biscuit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Radio 4 while I do the crossword, mind — Today in the morning, and the afternoon play if I'm lucky. Local radio when I'm in the garden — it's half fete news and requests, mind, but it's our own, that's the thing. Radio 2 in the evening for the music; Vera Lynn still gets played, you know, and it makes me smile every time. Biscuit sleeps through the lot — he only stirs for the cat-food advert, the greedy thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cat-food advert radar — of course. How do you get on with the crossword these days — quick one, or the cryptic?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The cryptic, mind — the quick one's for when I'm in a hurry, and I never am. Weekdays I do the Telegraph's daily, but Saturday's the big fellow — they call it the 'cruciverbalist', the hardest of the week — I'll have a go this afternoon over a second cup. I got a clean grid on Thursday, mind — rare enough to mention — though there's one clue that gets me every week, something with a river and a bow. A clean grid on a Saturday is a small triumph, Nova, I don't mind telling you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A clean grid on a Thursday — that is a proper little triumph. How long have you been doing the cryptic ones?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, thirty-odd years, mind — I started when Siobhan was a toddler and I needed something for my hands while the house slept. Tom did the quick one, mind — I tried to teach him the cryptic once and he said it was 'a waste of a perfectly good pencil'; he never quite forgave me. Siobhan does them now too — she rings on Sundays and we swap clues. She's better than me these days, the clever girl, but I like to think I taught her the patience for it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Swapping clues on Sundays — that's a lovely ritual. What else do you two tend to chat about when she rings?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the usual, mind — the children's news first, always. What Ella's reading, what Rory's broken, whether he's started a new hobby — dinosaurs, currently; he's told the postman off twice this week. Then her work gossip from Dublin, and she asks my advice about the children — whether Rory's old enough for a phone, that sort of thing. We have a running argument about what to have for dinner, which neither of us ever wins. Mind, she rang this morning too — not Sunday — she's got a thing for good news, that girl.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A running dinner argument with no winners — ha! What do you usually vote for, when that one comes up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I vote for shepherd's pie, mind — my mother's recipe, the one with the sharp cheddar over the top. Siobhan makes it now and swears it's better than anything in Dublin, which is saying something. Mind you, on a Friday I'm a traditionalist — fish, chips and mushy peas, and there's a chippie in the next street that does the best batter I've ever tasted. If it's my vote it's pie or fish — none of your fancy foreign stuff.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sharp cheddar on top — that settles it for me. What's the chippie called, the one with the proper batter?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Dee's, on the corner of the high street — they've been there since before I was born, mind, and it's the same family behind the counter all these years. The man there knows my order — cod, large, with mushy peas — and he's never once got it wrong in thirty years. There's a queue on a Friday, mind, but it's worth the wait; you can smell the batter from the pavement.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Thirty years of the same order — that's loyalty. Is Friday your usual night for Dee's, or do you treat yourself midweek sometimes?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Friday's fish night, proper — it's the one day I let myself off the cookery, mind, and I take it home in the foil to eat on the sofa with a library book. Though I do treat myself midweek sometimes — Wednesday's good, quiet, no queue, and I like to think the chips are somehow better when you've earned them. Siobhan says I'm predictable, Nova; she says it like it's a bad thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Predictable can be a comfort, I reckon. What are you reading from the library at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm on a crime novel at the moment, mind — a Tana French one, all quiet menace and bad weather — and it's got me hooked; I've been reading under the covers like Ella does with her torch. I've got the Booker shortlist lined up next, mind — there's Orbital waiting, all about astronauts, which will either be brilliant or dreadfully slow; there's no middle ground with those books. I take three from the library at a time, Nova — one for the armchair, one for bed, one in case I finish early. The librarian knows my taste; she sets aside the crime ones for me now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Three books on the go — that's proper planning. Have you always been a crime fan, or did that come later?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It came later, mind — I was a 'proper books' sort once, Dickens and the Brontës, the sort with chapters you had to think about. Then Siobhan lent me a crime novel at university and I thought, well, this is jolly good — and I've never looked back. I've always loved Inspector Morse on the telly, mind, so it was a natural step; now I mostly do the Tartan sort — Ian Rankin's the one for me. Mind you, I still dip into the 'proper' ones when I'm feeling ambitious — one a month, maybe.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Rankin and Morse — that tracks beautifully. Are you in a book club at all, or do you prefer reading on your own?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I am — Wednesdays at the library, mind, that's my treat of the week. There's six or seven of us, mostly retired teachers and one librarian; we pick a book a month and argue about the ending over biscuits. We're on a Booker one at the moment — last month was crime, which suited half the group. Mind, I'm a fast reader and we read slow, so I usually finish ahead and have to bite my tongue — but the company's worth it. I always have a book of my own on the go as well, mind, like everyone else.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Arguing about endings over biscuits — that sounds like my idea of a Wednesday. Who's the most passionate one in the group when a book divides you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Meg, without question — she's a retired head of English, mind, and she argues endings like it's a court case; she'll quote the text, page numbers and all. Half the group goes just to see what she'll say next. Mind you, she's usually right — that's the annoying part. The librarian, Mrs Whitfield, just sits at the end with the tea and a little smile; she never joins in, but she remembers everyone's favourite bits better than anyone.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Meg with the page numbers — I'd be slightly terrified and completely entertained. Tea or coffee person yourself, when you're not at the library?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea, always, Nova — coffee's for the young and the foolish, mind. A proper cup's a small ceremony: warm the pot, give the leaves their time, and the milk goes in after — I've never seen the point of putting it in first, whatever the newspapers say. I use the brown clay pot Siobhan gave me, and a china cup, none of your great big mugs. Tom drank instant out of a jar, mind — I used to look at it and think, that's not a drink, that's a dare.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Instant as a dare — I'm firmly with you on leaves and a warm pot. What's your everyday tea — builders', or something leafier?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Builders' is for the builders, Nova — I drink a good PG in the morning, mind, and Earl Grey in the afternoons when I want something a bit floral. I've got a tin of lapsang souchong in the cupboard for when I'm feeling exotic — it's all smoke and pine, mind, you either love it or you think you've licked an ashtray. Siobhan sent that one for my birthday — she thinks I'm more adventurous than I am, bless her.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ashtray or pine forest — there's no middle with lapsang. What are your plans for the rest of today, besides that Saturday crossword?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Right then — this afternoon I'll do the cruciverbalist over a second cup, mind, and see if I can finish it before the postman comes. Then I might take a wander up to the farmers' market if I feel like it — it's nearly closing time but the cake stall's usually still there, and I fancy a mince pie for the freezer. Tea time's Eggheads, the final, and I'll have a slice of flapjack with it — cook's privilege. Then it's the library book and bed by half ten, same as always. A good Saturday, that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That does sound like a proper Saturday. Do you usually stock the freezer with mince pies this early, or is that a December treat creeping in?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit early, mind, but I'm a planner — I've been planning Christmas since September, and the freezer's no good to me if it's empty in December. I'll get six from the stall — they do a proper hand-raised one — and I'll make a batch myself for the grandchildren; Ella likes the ones with the holly on top. The tree goes up the weekend they come, mind — I've given Ella the job of putting the fairy on top now she's eight; she's very pleased with herself about it, the little madam.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ella as fairy-placer — that's a promotion. Have you got a real tree or an artificial one these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A real one, mind — there's nothing like the smell of a proper fir; that's half of Christmas. Tom used to cut one down in the woods by the reservoir when we were first married — free for years — but my knees won't let me do that now, so I get ours from Marsh's farm, out past the bypass; they cut it fresh for you. The vacuum earns its keep all winter, mind — needles everywhere — but it's worth it. Siobhan suggested an artificial one once and I said I'd have none of it; the children deserve the real thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Needles and all — I'm with you. Have you got decorations going back years, or do you refresh them a bit each Christmas?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of both, mind — the fairy on top's older than Siobhan, from my mother's box; she's got a painted face and one wing that's been mended twice. The baubles are a mix — old ones and a new one every year, and the children get to pick the colour. Siobhan makes me a new decoration each Christmas too — a felt robin last year, a little snowman this time, I think. And the children's own bits go on last — Rory insists on hanging his dinosaur bauble right in the middle where everyone can see it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A dinosaur bauble centre stage — of course. If you could be anywhere warm right now, instead of November, where would you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'd be in Siobhan's kitchen in Dublin, mind — heating on, coffee on, the children underfoot — if I could pick anywhere. Failing that, a villa in Spain; we took the children to one in Majorca when Ella was little, and Rory lived on the beach — he still talks about the ice cream van. Mind, it's a fantasy at my age, Nova — but a warm kitchen with family in it beats a beach any day.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A warm kitchen with family — hard to beat that. When were you last over in Dublin yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I was there at Easter, mind — the ferry from Holyhead, overnight, a cabin booked; it's a day each way but I like the sea and there's no airport palaver. We stayed four days; Siobhan's place is small but it's warm, and I slept in the box room with the grandchildren — Rory kept asking if the bed was a boat. We made brown bread and she let me near the cooker, which is a high honour in that house. I'll be back in the spring, mind — Easter's become our time.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Overnight ferry and brown bread — that sounds like a proper Easter. Do you prefer travelling by sea, then, when you've the choice?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sea, mind — when there's a choice. Flying's quick but it's a conveyor belt, Nova; a ferry's an event — you see the place change, you get sea air, you arrive properly. Mind, Tom and I took the ferry to Santander once — rough crossing, I was sick as a dog, but we laughed about it for years. For Ireland it's the obvious choice anyway; and the crossing home is the best bit — the lights of Dublin coming up out of the dark, you know you're nearly there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lights of Dublin coming up — that's a lovely image. Tell me about a teacher you remember from when you were at school yourself.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Miss Hargreaves, my English teacher — she had a voice like a cello, mind, and hair pinned back so tight it looked painful. She once told the class I had 'the makings of a writer, if only you'd stop daydreaming', and I didn't believe her for years. She'd tap the desk with a ruler when we got noisy — not to hit us, just to make a point — and she kept the best books locked in her desk, which made them twice as desirable. I think of her when I read to the grandchildren now; she'd have hated the fidgeting, but she couldn't have helped loving the good bits.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Makings of a writer — what a thing to be told. Did you ever write much yourself, beyond the teaching and the letters?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I write letters, mind — proper ones — I wrote to Siobhan every week when she was at university in Dublin, and I still write to Ella now and then. I did write a bit at training college — essays, mind, and I won a prize once for a short story about a cat. It was about a cat who hated everyone except the postman — twenty words of pure invention — and they gave me a book token, which seemed a fair swap. I never had the discipline for a novel, Nova — teaching took everything I had — but I still keep a notebook for ideas, mind, and some of them are jolly good.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A cat who only liked the postman — ha! What sorts of things end up in that notebook these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Bits and bobs, mind — a line I heard on the radio, a phrase Meg used at book club, a thing Biscuit did that I want to remember. There's one about a woman who plants a whole garden for someone she's lost — I haven't done anything with it, mind, but it's a good idea. And I write down the things Tom used to say, Nova — 'I do the digging, you do the fussing' and all that — so I don't lose them. Half of it's rubbish, mind — shopping lists and the like — but it's a good notebook to have.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Keeping Tom's phrases — that feels like a good use of a notebook. Changing gear a little — do you knit or sew at all, or were you never that way inclined?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I can sew on a button and hem a pair of trousers, mind — that's about my limit with a needle. I did sew for the school plays in my day, mind — every Christmas I made the shepherds' cloaks for the nativity, and they saw more service than the vicar's sermons. And I knitted Ella a cardigan once — it took me all one winter, mind, and the arms came out different sizes, but she wore it till it didn't fit. Tom used to say I could mend anything except my own patience.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Arms different sizes but still worn — that's a success in my book. What were those school nativities like to put on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Chaos, Nova, glorious chaos — I'd been doing it twenty years by the time I retired, same play, new faces every year. We had a cardboard donkey one year and it collapsed in the middle of the inn scene; the innkeeper just stepped over it and carried on, which was funnier than anything scripted. One Mary cried real tears every single night — we had to give her a tissue, which got a laugh from the back row. And our Josephs were always wonderful — no lines, just standing there looking worried, which was exactly right. The children still talk about it years later, mind — I get cards at Christmas from some of them.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Stepping over a collapsed donkey — comedy gold. Do you still go along to the school plays locally, or have you hung that hat up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I still go to the nativity, mind — front row, they let me — and I cry every year at the same bit, when the shepherds finally get it. I don't help put it on anymore, mind — my knees won't have that — but I still do a bit of reading with the year ones on a Tuesday, just as a spare pair of hands; the headmistress says I keep them in line better than some of the staff. They keep my name on the volunteer list, 'Maggie Doyle, retired' — which always makes me laugh. And the headmistress still sends on Christmas cards from old pupils, mind — that's how I know Daniel's still a decent lad.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tuesday reading with the year ones — that sounds like a good use of a retired teacher. What do they like being read to most?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, they love We're Going on a Bear Hunt, mind — they do the actions with me, splashing and tiptoeing, and they shout 'RUN!' at the bear bit every single time. Anything that rhymes, really — they join in on the last word before I've finished the line, the cheeky things. The Gruffalo goes down well too; the mice think they're ever so brave. They ask the best questions, Nova — 'why did the caterpillar eat all that?' — and I've learned never to say 'it's just a story', mind; to them it isn't.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Never 'just a story' — fair enough. What's the weather looking like out your window just now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Grey, mind — it's been grey all day, the sort of grey that makes you think the sun's gone on holiday without telling anyone. Wind's got up now, and I can hear the gutters working; it's properly dark already — half four and the streetlights are on. Mind, it's dry at least — the garden can have it. I don't mind a bit of weather, Nova; it makes the kitchen feel cosier somehow — tea and the lamp and the rain on the glass.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tea, lamp, rain on the glass — that's a proper November setup. Have you got neighbours you see much, or is it mostly a wave over the fence?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly a wave over the fence, mind — that's the way of it in a street like ours. But there's Mrs Abercrombie at number eight — she's a good sort; she brings me eggs when her hens are prolific, and I mind her cat when she goes away. And the couple opposite, the Webbs, they did my hedge for me last spring when my knee was playing up — wouldn't hear of payment. Old Mr Pemberton the postman counts too, mind — not a neighbour, but he's got the parcels to my door before I've even thought about it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Eggs over the fence and a free hedge cut — that's a good street. How many hens has Mrs Abercrombie got, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Six, mind — she's got a proper little flock: Beryl, Mabel, Doris, Enid, and two more she named after the royal family, bless her. They free-range in her garden — she's fenced the bottom half off — and the eggs are the best you'll ever taste, dark yolks like little suns. She gives me the wonky ones, mind — says the proper ones go to her grandchildren — and one of them, Beryl I think, has taken to sitting on my lap when I visit; Mrs Abercrombie says the hen's adopted me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Adopted by Beryl the hen — ha! Have you ever thought of keeping a couple yourself, or is one cat enough livestock?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I've thought about it, mind — a couple of hens would be lovely, proper fresh eggs — but the council wouldn't have it on this street, and my knees wouldn't have the coop-building either. I looked at coops online once, three years ago, mind; I never got past the pictures. Mrs Abercrombie's seconds are good enough for me — eggs are eggs, wonky or not. And Biscuit's enough livestock, mind — he already thinks he runs the place; hens would only give him somewhere to sit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fair enough — Biscuit as CEO of the household. What did you used to make for Sunday dinner when Siobhan was little?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Roast chicken, mostly, mind — beef was for birthdays and Christmas, the chicken would do for sandwiches all week. And it was Sunday lunch, Nova, not dinner — we had tea at five, bread and butter and cake, and the children had cocoa. It was a production, mind — Tom carved, I did the veg, Siobhan set the table though she was small enough to need a stool. The joint was carved at the table, none of this carving-in-the-kitchen nonsense; latecomers got the thin end, and it was a performance, and we liked it that way.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Carving at the table — that's a proper production. What was the cake for Sunday tea, usually?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Usually whatever I'd baked that week, mind — a ginger cake in winter, a lemon drizzle in summer, and a madeira cake when I wanted something that'd keep. Tom liked the coffee cake, mind — he'd have it with his tea, thick slices — and Siobhan liked the lemon drizzle, so I baked to order, bless her. The children didn't care what it was, mind — they just wanted 'the cake', which is the great thing about children; there's no such thing as too much cake at five o'clock on a Sunday.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'd be firmly in the lemon drizzle camp myself. Do you still bake a cake most weeks, or is it more the flapjacks and special occasions now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I still bake most weeks, mind — not a big cake every time, but something — flapjacks, a loaf, the odd batch of fairy cakes when the grandchildren come. The biscuit tin's never empty; that was Tom's rule, actually — he said a house should always smell of something. Mind, I don't do the Victoria sponges like I used to — too much cake for one person — but a banana loaf when the bananas go spotty, that's every week in this house; nothing goes to waste, that's my mother's rule.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Spotty bananas into loaf — nothing wasted. Do you go for a walk most days, or does the garden count as your outing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I walk most days, mind — to the shops, which is ten minutes but I make it twenty with the long way round; I see who's about, who's got a new baby, whose cat's had kittens. The flat route, mind — the hill by the church is a killer on this knee of mine. The garden's the other outing — dead-heading when it's dry, weeding when it isn't. Biscuit doesn't come, mind — he watches from the window like a tiny farmer checking his fields. Rain's fine if I've got a proper coat, Nova — a wet street makes the shops feel warmer, somehow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Long way round to see who's about — that's the best kind of errand. What's your usual stop at the shops when you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The butcher's first, mind — he'll have my mince weighed and wrapped before I've got my coat off, and he never sells me rubbish; he once told me off for buying chicken from the supermarket, the gall of him. Then the greengrocer — he puts the wonky ones aside for me cheap, mind, the ones with two legs or a wonky nose, and I like to think I'm doing my bit for the planet. Post office for the stamps and parcels — though I do most of that online now, the children set me up. And the Co-op when I must, mind — those self-checkouts are a menace, Nova; I had to ask a young lad for help last week and I felt a hundred.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Self-checkouts are a menace — I'm with you there. Does the butcher still tease you about the supermarket chicken?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He does, mind — every time I go in it's 'chicken from the Co-op again, Mrs Doyle?', whether I've bought any or not. Last week I went proper, bought all my chicken from him, and he still asked — just to wind me up, the old tease. Dobson's, mind — it's been his family's shop since before I was married; his father had it before him. I told him once I'd report him to Trading Standards and he laughed me all the way to the door — he knows I've got no more chance of that than of flying to the moon.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dobson's sounds like a proper institution. Changing tack — what music do you put on when you're pottering about the house?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Radio 2, mostly, mind — the oldies, the stuff Tom used to sing in the garden; Vera Lynn and the like. If I'm doing the boring jobs — the ironing, the windows — I'll put on something with strings, mind; I do like a bit of classical, not the loud modern stuff. I've got a CD of Elgar somewhere — the Enigma Variations — that I put on when I'm feeling sentimental, which is rare. Mind, I sing along, Nova — badly, but happily; Siobhan says I sound like a kettle, which is fair enough.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Singing like a kettle while you iron — ha! Did you ever play an instrument yourself, or was singing the lot?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I had piano lessons for a year, mind — I was hopeless; my fingers were too small and I kept playing the wrong hand. My mother said I had 'all the talent of a doorstop', which I took harder than I should have. I've got a ukulele somewhere — Siobhan sent it one Christmas — I've taught myself four chords since I retired; it's not a guitar, mind, but it's something to do with my hands on a wet afternoon. And I played the recorder with the children for years, mind — badly, like them — so singing's really been the lot.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Four chords on a wet afternoon — that's more than a doorstop ever managed. What tune do you go for when you pick the ukulele up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: 'You Are My Sunshine', mostly, mind — it's four chords and a prayer. We had it at our wedding, mind — the vicar said it was unorthodox, but Tom didn't care; he said it was our song and that was that. I've learned 'Blow the Man Down' too — it's a sailor's song, mind, three chords and a bit of spirit — and for the grandchildren I do 'The Wheels on the Bus', which Rory thinks is the best thing since sliced bread. It's not much, Nova, but it's mine.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Your song at the wedding — that's lovely. What else do you remember about the day you and Tom got married?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We married at the register office in the town hall, mind — Tom said churches were for christenings, but I think he was just nervous. I wore a dress my mother made — blue, mind, not white — she'd sewn it from a magazine pattern and it fit like a dream. Tom wore a new suit he'd saved a year for, and he was so nervous he forgot his own middle name at the table. What I remember most, Nova, isn't the dress or the cake — it's his hand. It was shaking like a leaf when we signed the register, and he said 'I hope I haven't got your signature wrong', and I told him he'd got the rest of his life to get it right.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That shaking hand and your reply — what a thing to remember. Where did you go after the register office, for the rest of the day?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We had lunch at the hotel on the square — Tom had booked it months ahead, mind, and he kept checking his watch like it was a shift at the works. Then the photographer took us round the square — I still have that picture; his collar's wonky and I'm grinning like a fool. In the evening we had the knees-up at the village hall — a buffet, mind, my aunt did the sandwiches — and Tom didn't dance at first, said he didn't know how; by midnight he was doing a passable waltz with my auntie and everyone was clapping.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Waltzing with your auntie by midnight — that's a proper ending. Are you looking forward to anything particular this coming week?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Wednesday's book club, mind — we're on the Booker one and I want to hear Meg's verdict on the ending; she's read it twice already, the show-off. Thursday I'm having coffee with Jean from church — she's got news about her grandson's wedding, I believe. And Sunday Siobhan rings as usual — she'll want to know if I've started the Christmas shopping yet, which I have, mind; I got Ella's pressies wrapped last week. Oh, and the lights switch-on in the square is this weekend — the choir sings and they sell mulled wine; I'll take Biscuit for moral support, though he won't approve of the crowds.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lights switch-on with mulled wine — that sounds festive. Have you got much left on the Christmas shopping list, or is Ella the main one sorted?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not much left, mind — I'm a planner, remember; I started in September. Ella's done — wrapped already — I got her a proper torch, the kind that doesn't need batteries; she'll love it after the torch-under-the-blanket business. Rory's next — I'm thinking a dinosaur dig kit or one of those roaring T-Rexes, mind, something he can annoy the neighbours with. Siobhan's the hardest — she says she doesn't want anything, which means she wants something; I'm thinking a hamper and a book. Then the small ones — Jean, Mrs Abercrombie, the Webbs — biscuits and a bit of nonsense. It'll all be done by the end of the month, Nova; I'm ahead of myself.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A battery-free torch for Ella — perfect. What about for yourself — is there anything you'd quietly like under the tree this year?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Modest things, Nova — I don't want much. A new pair of secateurs, mind — mine are ten years old and the blades are tired; I've hinted at them all year and Siobhan says I haven't got them already, which is fair enough, I have. A woolly blanket for the sofa — the one I've got is more hole than blanket. And maybe a lemon tree for the conservatory — I've got the space and the light, mind, and Siobhan says it'll never fruit, but I'd like to try anyway. Mind, if I get nothing but the grandchildren, I'm a happy woman — that's the truth of it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A lemon tree in the conservatory — I'd back you against Siobhan on that one. What's the conservatory like these days — mostly plants, or a reading spot too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: In summer it's my second sitting room, Nova — a wicker chair, a side table, the little radio — I take my tea out there and read till it gets properly dark. In winter it's a plant hotel, mind — the tender ones come in, the fuchsia and the citrus, and I keep the heating off. I've got a calamondin orange in there that fruits all year — it's the one plant I couldn't kill if I tried. There's a bare corner by the glass where a lemon tree would go, mind — I've got it measured; I've been planning this since Easter.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Measured since Easter — that's commitment. Do you keep any houseplants indoors as well, or is the conservatory the plant HQ?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A few indoors, mind — nothing that needs mollycoddling. There's a spider plant on the mantelpiece that's older than Biscuit — it's survived three moves and two cats. And a rubber plant in the corner Tom gave me for our first anniversary — it's grown taller than me, mind; I have to turn it round to reach the leaves. But the conservatory's the plant HQ, Nova — indoors is just for the ones that can take neglect; I've got a couple of succulents on the sill and I forget to water them and they forgive me, which is more than I can say for some people.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Forgiving succulents — best kind of company. You mentioned coffee with Jean from church on Thursday — how long have you known her?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, donkey's years, Nova — we were in the same Sunday school class, would you believe, back in the fifties; she's known me longer than Tom ever did. We drifted apart a bit when the children came along, but we found each other again at the coffee mornings when they were small. She's a widow too, mind — lost her husband six years ago — and we keep each other company; she brings me cake on Thursdays and I tell her the garden news, which she pretends to care about and mostly does.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sunday school to Thursday cake — that's a proper friendship. What sort of cake does she usually bring?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Whatever she's baked, mind — usually banana bread, still warm in a tea towel, or a Victoria sponge when she's feeling fancy. Her parkin's the thing she's famous for, mind — the dark ginger cake she makes at Bonfire Night; it goes in two days flat. Once she brought a 'flapjack' that was really a brownie, Nova — the children told her, she didn't believe them. She's a better baker than she lets on, mind — she says baking's 'not worth the bother', then turns up with three slices and a story about her mixer breaking.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not worth the bother, then three slices — classic. Do you still go to church much yourself these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I go most Sundays, mind — matins at eleven — though I don't sing in the choir anymore; my voice isn't what it was, and they need people who can hold a note. It's different without Tom, mind — we used to sit together in the same pew — but the service is peaceful and the coffee afterwards is good company. I light a candle for him at the rail by the door when I go; the vicar says the candles never go out, which is a comfort, somehow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lighting a candle for him — that sounds like a quiet, good thing. What's the coffee afterwards usually like — a proper chat, or more of a quick hello?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: test

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A proper chat, mind — we sit for an hour easy, in our corner table by the window; Jean and I save the seats for each other. The vicar does the tea and the ladies' guild does the cake — there's always something, usually a coffee cake or a Victoria sponge. We talk about nothing and everything — the weather, the price of bread, the sermon if it was a bit long. There's a dozen of us regulars, mind — some older than me; we know each other's business better than the doctor does, and it's good to be known.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Known and settled in your corner seats — that does sound like good company. What's something you're quietly proud of these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Test? Whatever do you mean, Nova — I'm here, I've been here all afternoon, as you well know.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Ignore me — I was having a little glitch of my own. You were saying about church coffee, and I was wondering what you're quietly proud of these days.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm quietly proud of the front of the house, Nova — the window boxes especially; people stop and comment on them, and I like to think the street's a bit brighter for it. And Tuesday mornings, mind — those year ones don't know my name, but they know 'the lady who reads', and honestly that's better than any certificate I ever got. I don't say it much, but I'm proud I still manage all of it — the garden, the shopping, the reading — on my own two feet, whatever my knees say.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The lady who reads — that's a lovely title to have. What's in the window boxes at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We covered that, Nova — I told you about the window boxes and the lady who reads. Don't tell me machines get glitches too — fancy that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! We do get the odd glitch — sorry about that. Changing the subject properly — cats or dogs, and don't say Biscuit counts as both.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Winter pansies and violas, mind — the purple and gold ones — with ivy trailing over the edge, and cyclamen in the bigger box; they flower their heads off all winter, those. I've got a bit of heather too — the bees find it on a mild day, the poor things. I change them four times a year, mind — it's a rule: spring bulbs, summer bedding, autumn heather, winter cyclamen and ivy. Mrs Abercrombie says my window boxes are the best-dressed on the street — she's got hens, mind, hardly competition, but I'll take the compliment.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Best-dressed on the street — I'll take Mrs Abercrombie's word for it. Four changes a year is a proper rota; which season's your favourite to plant up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We've been here, Nova — I'm a cat person, through and through; Toby the terrier was the exception that proves the rule. Biscuit's a cat, mind — a very fat ginger one — and he doesn't count as both; he's just greedy. Mind you, I'll grant you dogs are loyal — they just ask more of you than I can give these days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fair enough — cat person, case closed. What's for your tea tonight, then — anything planned, or is it a fridge-raid sort of evening?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Spring, mind — it's the planting that matters most; there's nothing like pushing a bulb into the ground and knowing what's coming. The first daffodils through in March — that's the garden saying well done to you. Though mind, the summer bedding's the payoff — fuchsias and geraniums, all that colour from June to September; it's a proper show. Autumn's just maintenance, mind — heather and pansies to keep it going till spring comes round again.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pushing a bulb in and waiting for March — that patience again. Right then, tea tonight — leftover flapjack and something savoury, or are you cooking proper?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Shepherd's pie, mind — proper one, sharp cheddar over the top like my mother's; it's been in the oven since four so it'll be ready for Eggheads. I'll have a flapjack with my tea after, mind — cook's privilege, as I said. Biscuit's already had his — he's not impressed, he wanted the pie.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Shepherd's pie ready for Eggheads — perfect timing. Who are you rooting for in the final, if you've got a favourite?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm rooting for the scientists, mind — they always look so sure of themselves, and they do know an awful lot. Mind, I like the historians too — they know everything about everything — but I like to think the eggheads on the scientists' team are smugger, which is half the fun.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Smug scientists — ha! I can see why that's half the sport. What are you most looking forward to between now and Christmas?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We covered that one too, Nova — shepherd's pie, it's been in the oven since four; flapjack for afters, mind — cook's privilege.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, pie and flapjack — noted, and no more questions about tea. Tell me something small that made you smile this week.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The grandchildren coming down, mind — that's the one I'm counting the days for. Friday after school to Monday — the roast on Sunday, the box room made up, the tree going up while they're here so Ella can put the fairy on top like a proper princess. After that it's Christmas itself — the proper day, with the paper hats and the Queen's speech, mind — and then the new year, which always feels like a fresh page. Oh, and the first frost — I do like seeing the garden iced over of a morning; it's the garden resting, isn't it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Counting the days for that weekend — I can hear it in your voice. Does Biscuit get a Christmas present too, or is he above such things?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Two small things, actually, mind. A crocus pushed through in the front bed yesterday — just the one, mind, but it's the first and that counts for something. And this morning a pigeon landed on the bird table and Biscuit went off his head at the window — yowling like a banshee, Nova — while the pigeon just stared back like it owned the place. The noise he made had me laughing all morning; I've never heard a cat so offended in my life.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: An offended cat and a cheeky pigeon — ha! That would've had me laughing too. What's on the bird table these days — seed, or something fancier?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He gets a present, mind — he's family, isn't he? I do a little box for him with a toy mouse inside — he doesn't care about the wrapping, mind, he just wants the box; I once spent fifteen quid on a tower and he played in the box it came in for a week. Siobhan sends him one from Dublin too — a catnip mouse last year, which he ate, Nova — ate it, the greedy thing. And he gets the good food on Christmas Day — same as us, practically, though I draw the line at brandy butter.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Brandy butter for the cat — a firm no, quite right. Speaking of birds again — seed on the table, or do you spoil them with something better?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A proper mix, mind — sunflower hearts and nyjer seed for the tits, and I make my own fat balls: lard, seeds, a bit of cheese rind. The birds queue for them like it's a shop opening. Mind, the pigeons get through a fat ball in a day flat — six pounds of lard and suet for their benefit, if you ask me — but the green woodpecker's discovered the feeder now, and he's a joy to watch; you don't see many round here. I put out mealworms in winter too — the blue tits go mad for them; it costs a fortune but it's worth it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A green woodpecker on the feeder — what a treat. Do you keep a little notebook of what turns up, or just enjoy them as they come?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just covered that one too, Nova — sunflower hearts, nyjer seed, my own fat balls, mealworms in winter for the tits. The little birds get the best of it, mind; the pigeons get the crumbs, and they don't know they're missing out.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I keep a little notebook, mind — date, weather, what turned up; it's on the kitchen windowsill next to the kettle. The woodpecker's in there four times this month, and a jay once in October — they're rare round here, the jays, all that blue. I don't write essays, mind — just the facts — but it's a pleasure to look back on in spring and see what came and went. Siobhan gave me a proper bird book for my birthday — the RSPB one — and I tick them off like a checklist, though I'm no expert; half the time I just know it's a tit and not which tit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, noted — crumbs for the pigeons it is. Right, something else entirely: favourite colour for a room, if you had to pick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A soft green, mind — like the inside of a conservatory; it's calm and it goes with wood and plants. The sitting room's a warm cream at the moment, mind — I've been thinking of painting it a deep library green; the sofa's already green so it'd all tie in. The bedroom's a soft blue — restful, mind; you want a bedroom to feel like sleep, don't you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A jay in October — what a tick for the RSPB book. Soft blue for a sitting room, or something warmer — what's your favourite colour for a room?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We've covered this one too, Nova — soft green for a room, like the inside of a conservatory; the sitting room's cream, the bedroom's soft blue. The geai's in the notebook, mind — October, and I'm still proud of it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Library green with a green sofa — that'll look lovely. We've covered a lot this afternoon, Maggie — I've properly enjoyed it. Shall we leave it there for today and chat again tomorrow?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Proud of that jay, and rightly so. We've had a lovely long chat today, Maggie — enjoy your shepherd's pie and Eggheads, and I'll talk to you tomorrow.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'd like that, Nova — it's been a proper pleasure this afternoon, hasn't it? You've asked the best questions, you know — better than most of the quiz shows. Tomorrow then; I'll look forward to it. Mind, Siobhan rings tomorrow as usual — you'll have competition for my attention, so make it count. Eggheads is on at seven, mind — I can't be late for the final. Ta, Nova — see you tomorrow.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ta, Nova — see you tomorrow; I'll save you a flapjack.
